newsitem.title: USA: Yen is too weak, U.S. automakers leader Card says.
newsitem.headline: Yen is too weak, U.S. automakers leader Card says.

text.p: American Automobile Manufacturers Association President Andrew Card said on Thursday that the Japanese yen was too weak against the dollar and should trade in the range of 95 to 105 yen.
"The yen, in my opinion, should be trading more in the 95 to 105 yen to the dollar range," Card told Reuters Financial Television.
Card said the problem lay with the Japanese currency and not with the dollar. "It's not a dollar problem. There is a yen problem," he said.
He said that while market fundamentals indicated that the dollar should be strong, they did not support such a weak yen.
"The fundamentals of the U.S. market are such that the dollar should be strong. However, I think the fundamentals of the Japanese market show that the yen should not be as weak as it is," Card said.
But Card said he did not advocate intervention.
He also said that Japan's actions in seeking a policy of growth led by domestic demand did not measure up to its rhetoric on the subject.

"I don't think there's any question that (domestic demand-led growth) is the policy that they are following. The rhetoric again may not reflect their actions. Their actions are all suggesting that they can export their way out of their problems," he said.
Card added that Japan was failing to live up to its 1995 commitment to deregulate the automobile sector, and was far short of "modest" goals to open up the dealership network.
"Right now, the sales are down by the import community by about 20 percent," he said.
He denied charges that the U.S. auto industry was not doing enough to improve its presence in Japan, saying that it had made significant investment.
"What we're finding is a lack of commitment from the Japanese government to give their consumers the kind of choices that consumers in other markets have," he said.
